# Introduction

In this vignette, we explore methods to identify synergies (or antagonisms) 
between TFs. As a example dataset, we use a subset of an ATAC-seq dataset of 
A549 cells upon ligand-based activation of the glucocorticoid receptor (GCR), 
encoded by the NR3C1 gene.

First, we load the package and the dataset:

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(betterChromVAR)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
data("NR3C1example", package="betterChromVAR")
peakSE
motifMatches
```

The `peakSE` object contains ATAC peaks counts for each 6 samples, while the 
`motifMatches` object indicates which peak matches which of a selection of 29 
motifs. For discussion about how exactly to generate those kinds of input, see
the `r Biocpkg("betterChromVAR")` package.

# Deviation-based methods

Motif deviations, as for instance computed by the `r Biocpkg("betterChromVAR")`
package, quantify the relative accessibility of given DNA motifs across 
samples/cells. These motif scores are then use to inference the relative 
activity of the corresponding TFs, and can then be used for differential 
analysis across conditions. If you are not familiar with motif deviations, it 
is recommended that you read up on it, for instance the documentation of the 
`r Biocpkg("chromVAR")` and/or `r Biocpkg("betterChromVAR")` packages.

## Standard differential motif accessibility using betterChromVAR

First, we illustrate the effect of the treatment of GCR motif accessibility by
computing standard motif deviations, followed by differential testing with
`fitDeviations()`, a wrapper around `r Biocpkg("limma")` that moderates the
variance according to the number of motif matches
^[If you are not familiar with such differential testing, see the `r Biocpkg("limma")` documentation.]:

```{r}
dev <- betterChromVAR(peakSE, motifMatches)
dev
```

```{r}
fit <- fitDeviations(dev, design=~group)
DAA <- as.data.frame(limma::topTable(fit, coef=2))
DAA
```

The results show GCR as the most differentially-accessible motif between the 
conditions, as expected, closely followed by the mineralocorticoid receptor 
(MCR), which has a motif very similar to GCR. We could also look at the pattern
across samples for top motifs (e.g. using `r Biocpkg("sechm")`).

Note that the `DAA` table reports a `logFC`, because that is what 
`r Biocpkg("limma")` outputs, however these cannot be interpreted as 
fold-changes, and rather represent differences between the conditions.

## Testing for motif interactions

Having identified GCR as the main motif differentially-accessible across 
conditions, we now want to know whether these differences are particularly at 
sites that have both GCR and some other motif (or the opposite, particularly
at sites that do not harbor the other motif). Computationally speaking, we 
want to test whether the deviation differences at intersecting sites (i.e. 
sites that harbor both motifs) are significantly larger (or smaller) than at 
sites harboring either motif.

To this end, we first compute deviations for the GCR sites, split according to
whether they also harbor each of the other motifs (`both`), or not (`baitOnly`),
as well as for the sites that have the other motif but no GCR motif 
(`partnerOnly`):

```{r, message=FALSE}
idev <- getInteractionsDeviations(peakSE, motifMatches, bait="GCR", minCount=10)
table(rowData(idev)$set)
```

Next, we test for a significant interaction with respect to the bait motif. For
each partner motif, the interaction score is the difference between the 
deviation at sites with both motifs, and the sum of the deviations at sites with
each of the motifs alone (i.e. what would be expected if the two motifs acted 
independently and additively, thereby taking into account the response of the 
partner's own sites). We then test how this score differs between groups:

```{r}
res <- discoverMotifInteractions(idev, "group")
head(res)
```

We could plot these results in a kind of volcano plot:

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(res, aes(difference, -log10(adj.P.Val), size=overlap.N, label=motif)) + 
  geom_text() + theme_bw()
```

The `difference` column indicate by how much the response in the intersection 
(e.g. in sites that have both the bait and its interacting motif) differs from 
what is expected from the response in sites that have only one of the two 
motifs, and the columns `diff.baitOnly`, `diff.partnerOnly` and `diff.both` 
give the response in each set of sites. For example, since we established 
earlier that the  treatment increases accessibility of GCR sites, and the 
difference in the interaction with CTCFL is negative, we can conclude that 
CTCFL appears to prevent GCR from having a positive impact. In contrast, sites 
that have the JUND motif (in addition to GCR) appear to increase in 
accessibility more than those that do not, in line with the known interaction 
between GCR and JUN/FOS family members.

Note that the p-values are meant to be used for ranking candidates rather than 
as calibrated error rates -- they are far from calibrated (see below). 
Moreover, since the classes of sites are aggregated, the p-values indicate 
reflect the reproducibility across replicates, rather than the generalization 
across sites. For a test that accounts for the variability across sites and 
produces more calibrated p-values, see the last part of this vignette.

## Investigating motif interactions through distance decay patterns

Next, we will explore a bit more in depth those candidate interactions by 
investigating their dependence on the distance between the two motifs. To this
end, the `exploreMotifInteraction` function will produce deviations for the 
sites harboring only GCR, only the candidate partner, or both at given distance
intervals of each other.

Computing this requires the motifs themselves and the genome sequence, e.g.
^[To avoid having the genome as a dependency, the precomputed `didevs` are 
included in the example data.] :

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38)

# we precompute the betterChromVAR background to save computing time in case
# we check many interactions:
bg <- computeBackgrounds(peakSE, getBackgroundBins(peakSE))

# `motifs` is a list of motifs (e.g. a PFMatrixList, as provided in the example
# data); we look at two potential partners of GCR:
didevs <- lapply(c(JUND="JUND", CTCFL="CTCFL"), \(mo){
  exploreMotifInteraction(peakSE, motifs[c("GCR", mo)], bg = bg,
                          genome=BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38)
})
```

or each partner, we have deviations for
different subsets of sites, which we melt into a data.frame for plotting:

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
dd <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(didevs), \(mo){
  didev <- didevs[[mo]]
  d <- data.frame(feature=rep(row.names(didev), ncol(didev)),
                  group=rep(didev$group, each=nrow(didev)),
                  norm=as.vector(SummarizedExperiment::assay(didev, "norm")))
  d$feature <- factor(d$feature, row.names(didev))
  d$query <- mo
  d
}))
ggplot(dd, aes(feature, norm)) + geom_hline(yintercept=0, linetype="dashed") + 
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill=group)) + facet_wrap(~query, scale="free") + 
  theme_bw() + labs(x="Site type", y="Adjusted z-scores") + 
  theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle=90, hjust=1, vjust=0.5))
```

On the left of the first panel, we see the change in deviation upon 
ligand-based GCR activation (i.e. NR3C1 group vs CTRL) in sites harboring the 
GCR motif (independently of JUND status). Beside it, we see the same in sites 
harboring the JUND motif (independently of whether they also harbor a GCR motif),
which show no difference between conditions. Next, we see GCR sites that are
negative for JUND (which show a smaller impact that GCR sites more generally),
followed by JUND sites negative for GCR (i.e. sites in which the other motif is
neither present nor within the maximum distance). Finally, we see sites harboring both
motifs, at difference ranges of distance from each other. The exact distances
represent quantiles (so that each distance bin is equally populated) up to a 
maximum distance specified by the user.

We see that when sites have GCR and JUND motifs very close to each other, the 
difference in deviation is larger (i.e. the effect of GCR activation on 
accessibility is stronger), and that this decays with distance, as we would 
expect of a bona fide interaction. If the interaction is a physical interaction 
between the TFs, we would expect this to decay rapidly, otherwise it can decay
more slowly.

In contrast, the putative interaction (antagonism) with CTCFL shows an 
inconsistent distance pattern: CTCFL appears to suppress the effect of GCR 
activation both when close or distant to the GCR motif, but not in the middle 
bin of 220-299bp. This makes the putative interaction less likely to be a 
direct physical interaction, but does not exclude an indirect interaction.

<br/><br/>

# Peak-level analysis

The analyses above use the *sets* of sites as the unit of observation: the
deviation of a set is computed in each sample, and compared across samples. The
p-values therefore reflect how reproducibly a set of (fixed) sites differs 
between conditions, but not whether this generalizes across sites: a set of
sites that is not special in any way will still have some reproducible 
difference between conditions, simply because the sites respond differently
from one another. An alternative is to use the peaks themselves as the unit of
inference. This is what the `peakLevelMotifTests` and 
`peakLevelMotifInteractions` functions do: the differential accessibility 
(log2-fold-change) of each peak is first estimated, and these are then modeled 
as a function of the presence of the motif(s) while adjusting for the peak's 
accessibility and bias. The approach is related in spirit to motif activity 
response analysis (MARA, implemented in ISMARA), which models the signal of 
regulatory regions as a function of the motifs they harbor 
[@balwierz2014ismara], but differs in that motifs are here tested separately 
rather than jointly (for step-wise joint testing, see the 
`stepwisePeakLevelMotifTests()` function).

`peakLevelMotifInteractions` runs the differential analysis of the peaks itself,
while `peakLevelMotifTests` takes as input the results of a peak-level 
differential analysis provided by the user, along with the 
`SummarizedExperiment` it was run on. Both methods regress the peaks' logFC on
the presence of (one or combinations of) motif(s), as well as non-linear 
technical covariates. In both cases, each peak is weighted by the inverse of its
logFC variance (reflecting how robust the logFC is across samples), plus a 
between-peak variance (taking the heterogeneity across sites harboring a motif
into account). Finally, the variance is inflated to account for the 
correlation between peaks, as done by `camera()` in the `r Biocpkg("limma")` 
package.

Note that the peak-level functions are considerably slower than the deviation-
based ones, so consider using multithreading. Moreover, make sure to filter out
low-count peaks (e.g. using `edgeR::filterByExpr`) before using these methods.

### Peak-level differential motif accessibility

For each motif, `peakLevelMotifTests` tests whether the peaks harboring the 
motif change more (or less) between conditions than comparable peaks that do 
not harbor it. We first run a differential accessibility analysis of the peaks 
(here using limma-voom, but this could be any other method), and then provide 
its results to the function, along with the design matrix used to estimate the 
correlation between peaks:

```{r}
design <- model.matrix(~group, data=as.data.frame(colData(peakSE)))
y <- limma::voom(assay(peakSE), design)
dea <- limma::topTable(limma::eBayes(limma::lmFit(y, design)), coef=2, number=Inf, sort.by="none")
pk <- peakLevelMotifTests(peakSE, dea, motifMatches, design=design, 
                          minCount=10)
head(pk[,c("motif","N","difference","P.Value","adj.P.Val")])
```

Once more, the results indicate a strong response of the glucocorticoid receptor 
(GCR) and the highly similar MCR motif, as expected.

### Peak-level motif interactions

Similarly, `peakLevelMotifInteractions` models the log-fold-change of the peaks
as a function of the presence of the bait motif, of the partner motif, and of 
their interaction:

```{r}
res2 <- peakLevelMotifInteractions(peakSE, motifMatches, bait="GCR", 
                                   group="group", minCount=10)
head(res2[,c("motif","overlap.N","difference","se","P.Value","adj.P.Val",
             "partner.diff")])
```

In the above, `difference` is the interaction coefficient (on the log2 scale), 
and `partner.diff` is the effect of the treatment at sites with only the 
partner's motif.

# Comparison of the deviation-based and peak-level approaches

## Differential motif accessibility

We first compare the motif-level statistics obtained from the deviations (using
`fitDeviations`) to those of the peak-level approach:

```{r, fig.width=5, fig.height=4}
fit <- fitDeviations(dev, design)
tt <- limma::topTable(fit, coef=2, number=Inf, sort.by="none")
cmp1 <- merge(data.frame(motif=row.names(tt), t.deviations=tt$t, 
                         FDR.deviations=tt$adj.P.Val),
              data.frame(pk[,c("motif","N","t","adj.P.Val")]), by="motif")
colnames(cmp1)[5:6] <- c("t.peaks", "FDR.peaks")
ggplot(cmp1, aes(t.deviations, t.peaks, label=motif)) + 
  geom_hline(yintercept=0, linetype="dashed") + 
  geom_vline(xintercept=0, linetype="dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(size=N), alpha=0.5) + geom_text(check_overlap=TRUE, vjust=-1) +
  theme_bw() + labs(x="t-value (deviations)", y="t-value (peak-level)")
```

The two approaches are in close agreement.

### Motif interactions

A similar comparison for the two types of motif interactions analyses (both using
GCR as a bait) :

```{r, fig.width=5, fig.height=4}
cmp2 <- merge(res[,c("motif","overlap.N","t","adj.P.Val")], 
              res2[,c("motif","t","adj.P.Val")], by="motif",
              suffixes=c(".sample",".peak"))
ggplot(cmp2, aes(t.sample, t.peak, label=motif)) + 
  geom_hline(yintercept=0, linetype="dashed") + 
  geom_vline(xintercept=0, linetype="dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(size=overlap.N), alpha=0.5) + 
  geom_text(check_overlap=TRUE, vjust=-1) + theme_bw() + 
  labs(x="t-value (sample-level)", y="t-value (peak-level)")
```
Again the statistics are fairly strongly correlated. However, the 
deviation-based approach is much more liberal: it 
identifies `r sum(cmp2$adj.P.Val.sample<0.05)` motifs at an FDR<0.05, versus 
`r sum(cmp2$adj.P.Val.peak<0.05)` for the peak-level one 
(`r sum(cmp2$adj.P.Val.sample<0.05 & cmp2$adj.P.Val.peak<0.05)` in common). 
This is to be expected, since the deviation-based approach aggregates partially 
overlapping sites, whereas the peak-level one takes into account the 
heterogeneity of the signal across sites of a motif. Of the known interactors, 
JUND shows a strong signal in the sample-level analysis, but only a nominal one at the 
peak-level (P=`r signif(res2$P.Value[res2$motif=="JUND"],2)`). (Note that this
example is a small dataset with few samples and a limited number of peaks.)

### Behavior on random motifs

To illustrate the difference in calibration, we repeat the analyses with random
sets of peaks, which should not have any specific response nor interaction 
with GCR. The following shows the proportion of these random motifs that are 
nominally significant (P<0.05) with each approach:

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
nr <- nrow(peakSE)
rnd <- sapply(round(exp(runif(100, 6, 9))), function(n){
  x <- logical(nr)
  x[sample.int(nr, n)] <- TRUE
  x
})
colnames(rnd) <- paste0("random", seq_len(ncol(rnd)))
rnd <- cbind(GCR=as.vector(assay(motifMatches)[,"GCR"]), rnd)

ridev <- getInteractionsDeviations(peakSE, rnd, bait="GCR")
rres <- discoverMotifInteractions(ridev, "group")
rres2 <- peakLevelMotifInteractions(peakSE, rnd, bait="GCR", group="group")

data.frame(approach=c("deviations", "peak-level"),
           `% p<0.05`=c(sum(rres$P.Value<0.05),
                                 sum(rres2$P.Value<0.05)), check.names=FALSE)
```

Because these motifs have no true interaction with GCR, the proportion should 
be around 5%. The deviation-based approach is therefore clearly too liberal, 
while the peak-level approach is roughly calibrated. For these reasons, we 
recommend using the peak-level approach to identify interactions, and use the 
deviation-based approach only via `exploreMotifInteraction()` to investigate 
the dependence on distance.
